title: Help in goodness
hook: help one another in righteousness and mindfulness, not in sin (5:2)
tomorrow: Food of the People of the Book

segments.voice: Yesterday, the opening of al-Ma'idah: fulfill your contracts, the knots, 'aqd, you've tied. Your line was keep the contract. Did you keep one agreement to the letter? Day three hundred eighty-nine.

A friend calls late at night. I need a favor. Can you tell my boss I was with you yesterday? Can you lend me money, the thing you suspect is for that thing again? Can you help me get back at my ex? Loyalty pulls one way. Something else pulls the other. The second verse of al-Ma'idah gives a short rule for it, and a hadith turns that rule into something surprising.
screen: `A FRIEND CALLS LATE AT NIGHT.` → `I NEED A FAVOR.` → `LOYALTY PULLS ONE WAY.`

segments.voice: Verse 2 begins with the pilgrimage: its sacred months, its offerings, the pilgrims on their way. It warns the believers not to let resentment toward the people who once blocked them from the Sacred Mosque push them into aggression. Then comes the line, in Pickthall's words: "Help ye one another unto righteousness and pious duty. Help not one another unto sin and transgression." Two Arabic words carry it. Birr, righteousness, a wide, warm word for goodness, the same word used for kindness to parents. And taqwa, mindfulness of God, the awareness that keeps you careful. So the verse doesn't say help your friends. It says help with good. The direction matters more than the person. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari makes it vivid. The Prophet ﷺ said: help your brother, whether he is an oppressor or oppressed. The companions were puzzled. Helping the oppressed, they understood. But how do we help him if he's the oppressor? The Prophet answered: by stopping him. That's help, too. Sometimes the loyal answer to the late-night call is no, and then a different offer: I won't lie to your boss, but I'll help you talk to him. I won't lend you that money, but I'll drive you to the meeting. Another hadith, in Sahih Muslim, says whoever points someone to good gets a reward like the one who does it. So helping in goodness isn't only refusing. It's also cheering, driving, lending, showing the way.
screen: `RESENTMENT IS NO EXCUSE` · `BIRR AND TAQWA` · `HELP THE OPPRESSOR BY STOPPING HIM` · `POINT SOMEONE TO GOOD` · then, large: `HELP YE ONE ANOTHER UNTO RIGHTEOUSNESS.`

segments.voice: When the bell starts, think of someone in your life who's trying to do something good right now: study, get healthy, quit something, start a project, care for a parent. Picture what they're up against. Then ask: what's one concrete thing I could do to help? Not advice. Help. A ride, an hour, a meal, a message at the right moment. And if someone has asked you for help in something you shouldn't do, picture the better offer you could make instead. The bell holds the time.
Birr, a wide, warm word for goodness. Help one another in it and in taqwa, mindfulness of God, never in sin and aggression, from 5:2. Today's word.
Your line: help in good only. Today, give that one concrete help to someone doing something good, and when a favor would lead somewhere wrong, offer a better one. Day three hundred eighty-nine.

screen: `DAY 389 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: FOOD OF THE PEOPLE OF THE BOOK.`

howItsDone: Muslim teachers often cite 5:2 for mutual aid, volunteering and charitable cooperation, and for refusing help in wrongdoing, even to friends.

myth: 5:2 says help your friends, whatever they ask
it says help in righteousness and mindfulness, never in sin.
the Prophet said to help an oppressor

fork.setup: the Prophet says: help your brother, whether oppressor or oppressed. the companions ask how you help an oppressor. what does he answer?
fork.reveal: by stopping him from oppressing. holding someone back from wrong is a form of help (Sahih al-Bukhari).

original.note: Arabic: and help one another in righteousness and mindfulness (5:2).

trapdoor: what it means: help in the direction of good, and refuse help in the direction of harm, even to friends.
what a scholar hears: ta'awun, mutual help, set against birr and taqwa versus ithm and 'udwan; revealed in a pilgrimage setting that warns against resentment.
recall: a trust: anything placed in your care
